subtitle: A complaint that works
words.intro: Half of Germany rents, so half of Germany has a landlord, and each has a letter to write about a heating system. Tenant law is strict, and a well-made letter in the correct form can cost a landlord money.

grammar[0].fact: In Germany you may send such a letter by *Einschreiben*, registered post, and if you really want it to count, by *Einschreiben mit Rückschein*. Germans take this sort of thing seriously, and the mere sight of the yellow slip can cause a landlord to phone you.

grammar[1].blocks[1].note: The calmer the letter, the more frightening it is.
grammar[1].fact: A deadline is the heart of a German letter of complaint, and it must be a real date: *bis spätestens 15. Mai*. Without one, you have legally only expressed an opinion. With one, the other side is *in Verzug*, in default, and things start to cost money.

document.intro: A real rental contract from Hamburg, typed and signed in 1932. It’s very like the one you’d sign today, only shorter. You can read: who rents, what, for how much, and how you get out.
document.fact: Tenants in Germany are very well protected, and the three-month notice in this contract is still the normal rule for tenants today. In 1932 the rent was 429 marks a year. Your landlord will be pleased to tell you what that would buy now.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Write to the landlord about one thing in your flat. Use the phrases.
document.tasks[1].note: The defect and the date are your own.
reading.intro: The lift in Hofstraße 12 has been out of order for eleven weeks. Frau Huber, on the first floor, doesn’t need it. But Herr Yilmaz’s mother does. So Frau Huber has dictated a letter to the property manager, and she’s very pleased with the result. Maya has just added the date.
reading.photos[1].caption: Balkone: Der Vermieter hat zugesagt, sie nächstes Jahr zu streichen.
reading.fact: A German tenant may reduce the rent if the flat has a real defect, and there are long court-made lists of how much. But do it wrong and you can be evicted. So tenants’ associations, the *Mieterverein*, have more than a million members, each paying for good advice.
